question: What are HTTP status code ranges and what does each range mean?
title: HTTP Status Code Ranges
direct_answer: HTTP status codes are three-digit response codes from 100 to 599. The first digit gives the broad result: `1xx` information, `2xx` success, `3xx` redirection, `4xx` a request-side problem, and `5xx` a server-side failure. The full code gives the exact meaning.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `1xx Informational` — an interim response; processing or a protocol exchange is still continuing.
`2xx Successful` — the request succeeded; use the exact code to show what success produced.
`3xx Redirection` — the client may need another step, another URI, or a stored response.
`4xx Client Error` — something about this request or target prevents completion; it is not always a reason to blame the user.
`5xx Server Error` — the server failed while handling a request that appeared valid. Always read the full code, not only its range.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An HTTP status code is the standard summary at the start of a response. Valid codes run from 100 to 599. The first digit gives the broad class, and the whole three-digit code tells the exact result. Even if a client does not know a new code such as `471`, it can still treat it as a 4xx response.

`1xx` codes are interim responses. They appear before the final response; for example, `100 Continue` tells the sender to continue with the request content. `2xx` means the request succeeded, but the exact success still matters: `200 OK` usually returns a result, `201 Created` reports a new resource, and `204 No Content` sends no response content.

`3xx` means another step is involved. Some codes send the client to another URI, while `304 Not Modified` tells a client that its stored response can still be used. This is why 3xx should not be remembered only as “a redirect page.”

`4xx` means the request cannot be completed because of a condition connected to the request or target. Examples include invalid syntax (`400`), missing valid credentials (`401`), and a target that was not found (`404`). `5xx` means the server failed to fulfil an apparently valid request, such as a general failure (`500`) or temporary unavailability (`503`).

The range is only the first clue. An API client should use the exact status and the documented contract. An error body may add safe details, but it does not change `200 OK` from an HTTP success into an HTTP error. A 5xx code also does not automatically make a retry safe; the HTTP method and the API's retry rules still matter.

items.label: Class
items.detail: Something about the request prevents this operation from completing.

items.label: Exact code
items.detail: No current representation is found for the target, or the server will not disclose one.

beats.recallRule: Read the range, then the exact code, then the response details; the body adds detail but does not replace the status.

sections.title: How an HTTP client reads the result
sections.content:
A status code works in layers. The range is a rough category, the exact code is the protocol result, and the response headers and content add details for this occurrence. Generic software can understand the category, while application code can use the exact code.

For example, `404 Not Found` belongs to 4xx, but its specific meaning is about the target resource—not simply “the user made a mistake.” The body can name the missing order in safe terms. It cannot change that response into success. This separation lets browsers, gateways, caches, logs, and application clients agree on the outcome.

The same idea prevents unsafe retry rules. `503 Service Unavailable` often describes a temporary server problem, yet repeating a request that creates or charges something can duplicate work. A client must also consider whether the operation is safe or idempotent and whether the API supplies an idempotency key or a documented retry policy.

sections.title: Read a status from broad outcome to exact meaning
sections.content:
| Range | Meaning | Representative codes | Typical next step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `1xx` | Interim information | `100`, `101` | Continue protocol exchange |
| `2xx` | Successful result | `200`, `201`, `204` | Consume result or continue |
| `3xx` | Redirect or representation reuse | `301`, `304`, `307` | Follow rules for that exact code |
| `4xx` | Request-side condition | `400`, `401`, `404`, `409` | Correct, authenticate, or stop |
| `5xx` | Server-side failure | `500`, `502`, `503`, `504` | Fail safely; retry only when allowed |

sections.title: The status and the body answer different questions
sections.content:
```http
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "code": "ORDER_NOT_FOUND",
  "message": "No order exists with id 42"
}
```

The status says that the target was not found. The JSON gives this API's safe, machine-readable detail.

sections.title: Classify before choosing the exact code
sections.content: Classify these results before choosing the exact code: invalid JSON, a newly created order, an unchanged cached page, and temporary server overload. The answers should be 4xx/400, 2xx/201, 3xx/304, and 5xx/503.

question: What is the difference between 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden?
title: 401 vs 403 Status Codes
direct_answer: `401 Unauthorized` means the request does not have acceptable authentication credentials; the response must include a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge. `403 Forbidden` means the server understands the request but refuses to perform it, often because the signed-in user lacks permission.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `401 Unauthorized` — acceptable authentication credentials are missing or were rejected.
A 401 response must send at least one `WWW-Authenticate` challenge.
`403 Forbidden` — the server understands the request but refuses to perform it.
In most APIs: 401 means “authenticate again”; 403 means “this identity is not allowed.”
A server may answer with 404 instead of 403 when confirming the resource exists would reveal sensitive information.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`401 Unauthorized` means the request does not have valid authentication credentials for the protected resource. The name is old and slightly confusing: it usually means “you are not authenticated here,” not “you are authenticated but unauthorized.” The response must include a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge that tells the client which authentication scheme applies.

`403 Forbidden` means the server understood the request but will not perform it. The most common API example is a user with a valid login who lacks the required role, ownership, tenant membership, or account state. HTTP does not require every 403 caller to be authenticated, so “logged in but not allowed” is a useful everyday rule, not the complete protocol definition.

Suppose `GET /account` arrives with no bearer token or with an expired token. The API returns 401 and a Bearer challenge; a new login or token may let the request pass. If a normal member calls `GET /admin/audit-log` with a valid token, the API returns 403 because that identity is not allowed to read the audit log. Supplying the same token again will not change that result.

There is one important security boundary. A server may return `404 Not Found` instead of 403 when admitting that a protected resource exists would leak information. Whether it returns 403 or a concealed 404, the authorization check must still happen. Keep the public message safe, and never omit the required challenge from a 401 response.

beats.spokenText: `401 Unauthorized` means the request does not have valid authentication credentials for the protected resource. The name is old and slightly confusing: it usually means “you are not authenticated here,” not “you are authenticated but unauthorized.” The response must include a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge that tells the client which authentication scheme applies.

beats.cue: Explain 403 without oversimplifying it
beats.spokenText: `403 Forbidden` means the server understood the request but will not perform it. The most common API example is a user with a valid login who lacks the required role, ownership, tenant membership, or account state. HTTP does not require every 403 caller to be authenticated, so “logged in but not allowed” is a useful everyday rule, not the complete protocol definition.

beats.spokenText: Suppose `GET /account` arrives with no bearer token or with an expired token. The API returns 401 and a Bearer challenge; a new login or token may let the request pass. items.detail: Credentials are missing, expired, invalid, or otherwise unacceptable; send a WWW-Authenticate challenge.

items.label: 403 Forbidden
items.detail: The request is understood, but authorization or another policy does not permit it.

beats.cue: Protect information about sensitive resources
beats.spokenText: There is one important security boundary. A server may return `404 Not Found` instead of 403 when admitting that a protected resource exists would leak information. Whether it returns 403 or a concealed 404, the authorization check must still happen. Keep the public message safe, and never omit the required challenge from a 401 response.
beats.recallRule: 401 challenges authentication; 403 refuses the understood request; 404 can conceal a forbidden resource.

sections.title: Two checks protect a resource
sections.content:
A protected request usually passes through two separate checks. Authentication asks, “Can the server accept these credentials and establish an identity?” Authorization asks, “May this identity perform this action on this resource?” Keeping those checks separate makes both the API response and the security log easier to understand.

The first check can happen at a gateway, a security filter, or the application itself. If the credentials are absent or unacceptable, processing stops with 401 and a challenge. After an identity is established, policy may check a role, record owner, tenant, subscription, or account state. A failed policy check normally produces 403.

With bearer tokens, RFC 6750 also uses the `WWW-Authenticate` response header to carry safe error information such as `invalid_token` or `insufficient_scope`. The API should not turn that header into a detailed security report: public responses should reveal only what the client needs to recover safely.

sections.title: Choose between 401, 403, and a concealed 404
sections.content:
```mermaid
%%{init: {"flowchart": {"curve": "linear", "padding": 6, "nodeSpacing": 12, "rankSpacing": 20}}}%%
flowchart LR
  R[Protected request] --> C{Credentials accepted?}
  C -- No --> U[401 + challenge]
  C -- Yes --> P{Action allowed?}
  P -- Yes --> H[Continue]
  P -- No --> F[403, or 404 when concealment is policy]
```

sections.title: Two different failures at one API
sections.content:
**Case 1 — credentials are missing**

```http
GET /account HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="account-api"
```

**Case 2 — the identity lacks permission**

```http
GET /admin/audit-log HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer valid-member-token

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
```

sections.title: Check what a new credential would change
sections.content: A missing or expired token for `/account` should lead to 401 plus a challenge. A valid member token for an admin-only endpoint should lead to 403. If the endpoint must not reveal whether the record exists, the same policy refusal can be exposed as 404.

question: When do you return 200 OK vs 201 Created vs 204 No Content?
title: 200 vs 201 vs 204 Status Codes
direct_answer: Use `200 OK` when a completed request returns useful content, `201 Created` when the completed request created one or more resources, and `204 No Content` when the request succeeded but there is no response content to send. Choose from the result, not from the HTTP method alone.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `200 OK` — the request succeeded and the response normally carries a useful result.
`201 Created` — processing finished and created one or more resources.
For 201, `Location` can identify the main new resource; without it, the request URI identifies that resource.
`204 No Content` — the request succeeded and the response ends after its headers; there is no JSON body.
The verb does not decide the status: PUT can return 201, 200, or 204 for different outcomes.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
All three codes mean success, but they promise different results. Start with two questions: did this request create a resource, and does the response contain a representation? Do not choose a code only because the request used GET, POST, PUT, or DELETE.

Use `200 OK` when the work is complete and the response returns useful content. A successful `GET /orders/42` can return order 42. An update can also return 200 with the updated order, and a POST that runs a calculation can return 200 with the calculated result even though it created no resource.

Use `201 Created` when the request has completed and created one or more resources. After `POST /orders`, a `Location: /orders/42` header can point to the main new order, and the body may contain its representation. A Location header is useful but is not required in every 201; if it is absent, the request URI identifies the primary created resource. PUT may also return 201 when it creates the target for the first time.

Use `204 No Content` when the work is complete and nothing needs to be sent in the response content. It is common after a delete or an update where the client already has what it needs. Headers such as `ETag` may still describe the resulting state, but a 204 response cannot contain JSON or any other message content.

A PUT to `/profiles/42` shows the full choice. If it creates profile 42, return 201. If it replaces an existing profile and sends the new representation, return 200. If the update succeeds with no content, return 204. If work has only been queued and is not complete, use `202 Accepted` instead of any status that promises completion.

beats.cue: Choose from the result rather than the verb
beats.spokenText: All three codes mean success, but they promise different results. Start with two questions: did this request create a resource, and does the response contain a representation? Do not choose a code only because the request used GET, POST, PUT, or DELETE.

An update can also return 200 with the updated order, and a POST that runs a calculation can return 200 with the calculated result even though it created no resource.

After `POST /orders`, a `Location: /orders/42` header can point to the main new order, and the body may contain its representation. A Location header is useful but is not required in every 201; if it is absent, the request URI identifies the primary created resource. PUT may also return 201 when it creates the target for the first time.

beats.spokenText: Use `204 No Content` when the work is complete and nothing needs to be sent in the response content. It is common after a delete or an update where the client already has what it needs. Headers such as `ETag` may still describe the resulting state, but a 204 response cannot contain JSON or any other message content.

If the update succeeds with no content, return 204. If work has only been queued and is not complete, use `202 Accepted` instead of any status that promises completion.
beats.recallRule: Created means 201; completed with content means 200; completed without content means 204.

sections.title: Design the success contract around what happened
sections.content:
The HTTP method tells the server what the client wants. The response status tells the client what actually happened. That small distinction explains why hard rules such as “POST is always 201” and “DELETE is always 204” fail. POST may run an action without creating a resource, while PUT may create one.

A useful API contract also tells the client where a created resource lives. In a 201 response, `Location` identifies the primary new resource when the server sends that header. `Content-Location` has a different meaning: it identifies the resource represented by the response content. The values can match, but the headers do not mean the same thing.

A 204 response is deliberately empty. The client should process its headers and stop; it should not try to parse a body. If an update needs to return the changed object, warnings, or another representation, 200 is the clearer choice. If the request only entered a queue, 202 says that processing has not finished yet.

sections.title: Choose by outcome and response content
sections.content:
| Status | What happened | Response content | Typical example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `200 OK` | Request succeeded | Usually a representation | GET result or updated resource |
| `201 Created` | One or more resources were created | May describe the result | Create an order; Location can name it |
| `204 No Content` | Request succeeded | No content/body | Delete or update with nothing to return |

sections.title: A creation response and an empty update response
sections.content:
**Created resource**

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /orders/42
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": 42, "status": "pending"}
```

**Successful update with no response content**

```http
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
ETag: "order-v2"
```

sections.title: Choose the response for each outcome
sections.content: For `PUT /profiles/42`, choose 201 when the profile is created, 200 when an existing profile is changed and returned, and 204 when it is changed with no response content. Choose 202 instead if the update has only been accepted for later work.

question: When do you use 400 Bad Request vs 404 Not Found vs 409 Conflict vs 422 Unprocessable Entity?
title: 4xx Status Code Distinctions
direct_answer: Use `400 Bad Request` for a broad request error, `404 Not Found` when the target is missing or deliberately hidden, `409 Conflict` when the request clashes with the resource's current state, and `422 Unprocessable Content` when the content type and syntax are valid but the instructions still cannot be processed.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `400` — the server sees a broad client-side request error, such as broken JSON or invalid message framing.
`404` — the target has no current representation, or the server chooses not to reveal one.
`409` — the operation conflicts with the target resource's current state.
`422` — the server understands the content type and syntax but cannot process the instructions inside it.
Use a more exact code such as `412` or `415` when its defined condition is the real problem. Keep the API's 400-versus-422 validation rule consistent.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
These codes point to different places where a request can fail. `400` is about a broad problem with the request itself. `404` is about the target. `409` is about the target's current state. `422` is about validly formed content whose instructions cannot be processed. Choosing the code by that boundary is clearer than treating every client error as 400.

Use `400 Bad Request` when the server cannot or will not process the request because it sees a client error. Broken JSON is the simplest example: the server cannot even read the intended object. Invalid message framing and deceptive routing also fit 400. If the real problem is an unsupported `Content-Type`, `415 Unsupported Media Type` is more exact.

Use `404 Not Found` when the target has no current representation, such as `GET /orders/999`. The code can also hide a forbidden resource when confirming its existence would leak information. A 404 does not say the target is gone forever; use `410 Gone` when the server knows the removal is permanent and wants to say so.

Use `409 Conflict` when the request makes sense but clashes with the resource's current state. An order that is already shipped cannot be moved back to draft, so the client may need to fetch the current order and choose another action. If an explicit `If-Match` condition failed, `412 Precondition Failed` is the more precise response.

Use `422 Unprocessable Content` when the server understands the content type, the syntax is correct, but the instructions cannot be processed. For example, a well-formed order containing `quantity: 0` may receive 422 if the API uses that code for domain validation. The older name “Unprocessable Entity” is still common, but RFC 9110 calls it “Unprocessable Content.”

An API may use 400 for all validation errors, or reserve 422 for syntactically correct requests that fail field or business rules. Both approaches can work. The important part is to document one rule, return stable error details, and prefer a more specific HTTP code when it exactly matches the failure.

beats.cue: Locate the failure before choosing a number
beats.spokenText: These codes point to different places where a request can fail. `400` is about a broad problem with the request itself. `404` is about the target. `409` is about the target's current state. `422` is about validly formed content whose instructions cannot be processed. Choosing the code by that boundary is clearer than treating every client error as 400.

beats.spokenText: An API may use 400 for all validation errors, or reserve 422 for syntactically correct requests that fail field or business rules. Both approaches can work. sections.title: How 400, 404, 409, and 422 mark different failures
sections.content:
A useful way to classify these failures is to ask which boundary stopped the request. The server first needs a usable HTTP message and a supported media type. It may then need to find a target resource. After that, an HTTP precondition, the resource's current state, or the meaning of the submitted instructions can still stop the operation.

Each boundary tells a different story. Broken JSON can produce 400, while an unsupported `Content-Type` has the more precise 415 response. An unknown order ID can produce 404 when that existing target is required. A failed `If-Match` condition maps to 412. A valid order that is already shipped can stop a move-to-draft request at 409. A new order with valid JSON but an impossible quantity can produce 422 under an API that reserves 422 for domain validation.

The diagram is a classification guide, not a universal execution pipeline. Some requests create a target instead of looking one up, and an API can discover checks in a different order. Use the most precise status for the actual failure, then add stable problem codes and field errors so the client can recover without comparing changing English messages.

sections.title: Match the failed boundary to the exact status
sections.content:
```mermaid
%%{init: {"flowchart": {"curve": "linear", "padding": 6, "nodeSpacing": 12, "rankSpacing": 20}}}%%
flowchart TD
  R[Match the failed boundary] --> M[Message]
  R --> T[Required target]
  R --> C[Condition]
  R --> I[Instructions]
  M --> B[400: syntax or framing]
  M --> X[415: unsupported media type]
  T --> N[404: absent or hidden]
  C --> P[412: precondition]
  C --> K[409: current state]
  I --> U[422: understood, not processable]
```

sections.title: A valid JSON request with an invalid business value
sections.content:
```http
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/invalid-order",
  "title": "Order cannot be processed",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "One or more order fields violate business rules.",
  "errors": [{"field": "quantity", "code": "must_be_positive"}]
}
```

sections.title: Classify four order failures
sections.content: Broken JSON maps to 400. An unknown order ID maps to 404. Moving a shipped order back to draft maps to 409. A well-formed new order with `quantity: 0` can map to 422 under the documented validation policy.

question: How do you implement consistent error responses in Spring Boot?
title: Spring Boot Error Response Design
direct_answer: Create one public error contract, then map failures to it in a shared `@RestControllerAdvice`. Use focused `@ExceptionHandler` methods, return the correct HTTP status with a safe `ProblemDetail`, keep private diagnostics in server logs, and test every path that can produce an error.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use one common set of public fields for errors; add documented fields only when a problem needs them.
Use `@RestControllerAdvice` and focused `@ExceptionHandler` methods to translate known application failures.
Use `ProblemDetail` for the standard fields. In Spring Boot 3.3, enable Problem Details for built-in MVC exceptions with `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true`.
Map the meaning of the failure to HTTP, align Spring Security errors, and never expose stack traces, SQL text, secrets, or internal class names.
Test status, `application/problem+json`, fields, required headers, and information leakage through the web layer.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A consistent error response means that the same kind of failure has the same HTTP status and the same common JSON fields across the API. In Spring MVC, `@RestControllerAdvice` is a shared place for this translation. A service can throw a meaningful exception such as `OrderNotFoundException`, and one focused `@ExceptionHandler` can turn it into the public response. Controllers no longer need their own copies of error-building code.

Choose the status from what failed. A missing order maps to `404 Not Found`; an update blocked by the order's current state can map to `409 Conflict`; and an unknown bug becomes a safe `500 Internal Server Error`. In Spring Boot 3.3, `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true` enables Problem Details support for built-in Spring MVC exceptions. Custom domain failures still need deliberate handlers. Authentication and access failures can occur before MVC, so Spring Security's entry point and access-denied handler must follow the same public contract.

Spring's `ProblemDetail` represents the standard RFC 9457 problem fields. `type` identifies a stable kind of problem, `title` is a short summary, `status` matches the HTTP response, `detail` safely explains this occurrence, and `instance` can identify this request or path. An extension such as `code: ORDER_NOT_FOUND` or a list of field errors is useful only when its name and shape stay documented.

The client response and the server log serve different readers. The response should contain enough information to recover, but it should not expose stack traces, SQL messages, secrets, internal host names, or Java package names. Store those diagnostics in protected logs with a request or correlation ID. A catch-all handler is a final safety net, not a replacement for clear handlers for expected failures.

Tests should call the real web layer and verify the full contract: status, `application/problem+json`, required fields, extension fields, and important headers. Cover malformed JSON, invalid input, a missing resource, a state conflict, authentication, access denial, and one unexpected exception. Add an assertion that private exception text never appears in the response.

beats.cue: Start with one public contract for the whole API
beats.spokenText: A consistent error response means that the same kind of failure has the same HTTP status and the same common JSON fields across the API. In Spring MVC, `@RestControllerAdvice` is a shared place for this translation. A service can throw a meaningful exception such as `OrderNotFoundException`, and one focused `@ExceptionHandler` can turn it into the public response. Controllers no longer need their own copies of error-building code.

beats.cue: Give every failure path a clear owner
beats.spokenText: Choose the status from what failed. A missing order maps to `404 Not Found`; an update blocked by the order's current state can map to `409 Conflict`; and an unknown bug becomes a safe `500 Internal Server Error`. In Spring Boot 3.3, `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true` enables Problem Details support for built-in Spring MVC exceptions. Custom domain failures still need deliberate handlers. Authentication and access failures can occur before MVC, so Spring Security's entry point and access-denied handler must follow the same public contract.

beats.cue: Explain the purpose of each problem field
beats.spokenText: Spring's `ProblemDetail` represents the standard RFC 9457 problem fields. `type` identifies a stable kind of problem, `title` is a short summary, `status` matches the HTTP response, `detail` safely explains this occurrence, and `instance` can identify this request or path. An extension such as `code: ORDER_NOT_FOUND` or a list of field errors is useful only when its name and shape stay documented.

support.title: Each problem field has one job

items.label: type
items.detail: A URI that identifies the same kind of problem across occurrences.

items.label: title + status
items.detail: Give the short problem name and the matching HTTP response status.

items.label: detail
items.detail: Gives a safe human-readable explanation of this occurrence.

items.label: instance
items.detail: Points to this occurrence, often with the request path; a separate safe request ID can connect it to logs.

beats.stage: Test the response, not only the method
beats.spokenText: Tests should call the real web layer and verify the full contract: status, `application/problem+json`, required fields, extension fields, and important headers. Cover malformed JSON, invalid input, a missing resource, a state conflict, authentication, access denial, and one unexpected exception. Add an assertion that private exception text never appears in the response.
beats.recallRule: One contract, clear failure owners, correct HTTP status, safe public detail, protected diagnostics, and web-layer tests.

sections.title: Build the error path as carefully as the success path
sections.content:
An API error is part of the public contract. The HTTP status gives general HTTP software the outcome. The problem body gives this application's stable problem type and safe details. Returning `200 OK` with an error flag breaks that agreement because gateways, monitoring, clients, and caches still see a successful HTTP response.

Spring MVC offers several exception boundaries. A focused `@ExceptionHandler` can handle one expected domain failure, and `@RestControllerAdvice` shares handlers across controllers. For built-in MVC exceptions, Spring Boot 3.3 enables framework Problem Details support when `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true`; extending `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` is useful when the application needs to customize those responses. A local controller handler has narrower scope, and Spring Security handles failures raised before a controller. The design is consistent only when each path has an owner and all owners produce the same common fields.

`ProblemDetail` is a container for the standard RFC 9457 fields and optional extension properties. The type should stay stable for the kind of problem; detail can change for the current occurrence. Spring uses the `status` value as the HTTP status, prefers a problem media type during content negotiation, and can use the current request path as `instance` when the application did not set one.

Known application failures should have deliberate mappings. A missing order becomes 404, a state conflict becomes 409, and invalid input normally becomes the API's documented 400 or 422 response. Security failures must keep required authentication headers. Unknown failures become a generic 500 response, while the actual exception stays in protected logs.

The last step is contract testing. Calling the real MVC or integration layer checks serialization, status, media type, headers, and exception resolution together. A direct unit test of the handler method cannot prove all of those behaviors.

sections.title: Different failures, one public response contract
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  R[HTTP request] --> S{Where does it fail?}
  S -->|Security filter| G[Security error handler]
  S -->|Binding or validation| M[Spring MVC exception handler]
  S -->|Domain rule| A["@RestControllerAdvice"]
  G --> P[HTTP status + ProblemDetail]
  M --> P
  A --> P
  P --> C[Consistent client response]
  G --> L[Protected diagnostics]
  M --> L
  A --> L
```

sections.title: Map one failure, then test the public response
Prove that every path speaks the same error language
sections.content: Call two endpoints that can miss an order and assert the same 404 problem structure. Then test unreadable JSON, validation failure, a state conflict, missing credentials, denied access, and an unexpected exception. Check required headers and confirm that stack traces, SQL text, and secrets never reach the body.
